source.title: Residual Matrix Transformers: Scaling the Size of the Residual Stream

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some text and equations have minor extraction/OCR artifacts, but the relevant results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses Chinchilla-optimal token counts for its model series, but it does not test the claimed loss power laws, extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its experiments investigate a new residual-stream scaling axis.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training-loss scaling curves, dev-loss changes from expanding the residual stream, resource comparisons, and downstream evaluations. These do not test the specified versions: the loss curves are training loss rather than held-out loss over the claimed parameter/token/compute scaling axes; residual-stream size is a different axis; and the downstream comparison does not test predictability from scale or pretraining loss. The Chinchilla token counts are used to set training runs, not reported as an optimization test.
record.test_reason: An architecture paper on Residual Matrix Transformers. It sets token budgets with the Chinchilla 20×params rule and plots 'scaling law curves' (Fig. 2) only to compare RMT with the Transformer. It fits no exponents, makes no extrapolation, does no fixed-compute allocation search, and does not relate downstream results to scale or loss. Its new axis, residual-stream size, is not parameters, tokens or compute.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also present residual-stream size as a new scaling axis. They claim that expanding it improves compute, parameter and data efficiency, and that RMT beats a 33% larger transformer downstream. They name runtime as the main limitation.
record.recipe_differences: This is an architectural study of Residual Matrix Transformers, not a reproduction of the original scaling-law fits. It trains on OpenWebText and investigates residual-stream size; model-size series use token counts described as Chinchilla-optimal.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that RMT runtime is a limitation: it takes 7.17s per train step versus 4.06s for the Transformer, and attributes the slowdown in part to tensor contractions replacing optimized GEMM operations.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed parameters and FLOPs (<1% difference), raising RMT residual-stream size from 384 to 4096 monotonically lowers dev loss. Residual 4096 reaches the residual-768 final loss with 23% fewer FLOPS and 25% fewer tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In RMTs, residual-stream size is an independent axis whose increase lowers loss at fixed parameters and compute.

fits_no_version.finding: RMT reaches the Transformer's minimum train loss (3.03) with 25% fewer parameters, 58% fewer FLOPS and 41% fewer tokens, but takes 4% longer in wall-clock time. At 6B tokens it has lower train and dev loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The RMT architecture shifts the loss-vs-resource curves relative to the Transformer at 46M–405M scale.

fits_no_version.finding: The 305M RMT beats the 405M Transformer on all reported zero-shot perplexity and accuracy tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RMT outperforms a larger Transformer downstream at matched token count.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 267, 2025
record.problems: The paper says resource constraints prevented exploring whether the model-size trends continue at larger sizes. The core comparisons use models up to 405M parameters and 6B tokens. Scaling curves do not report fitted exponents or prediction errors for held-out runs. Uncertainty estimates are not reported for the listed results. The paper also identifies runtime as a limitation.
record.rows_left_out: No reported table or figure results directly test a claim version, so no tested-version rows were omitted. Numerical rows for all separately reported downstream datasets are retained.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of held-out loss. Fig. 2 plots train loss against parameters and FLOPS over about one order of magnitude (46M–405M), with no exponents.
No fit on small runs is used to predict larger runs.
Token budgets are fixed by the Chinchilla 20× rule. There is no search for the compute-optimal split.
No depth or width sweep of a standard transformer at fixed parameters. The RMT Dk sweep is a different architecture dimension.
The downstream comparison covers two models only, with no relation to scale or loss.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

missing.what: Fig. 2 train loss vs FLOPS and vs parameters for both 4-model series (46M–405M) at Chinchilla-optimal tokens. It is figure-only with no fitted exponents. Record it only as descriptive, since it is not a test of V1.

Transformer-variant comparison (Table 10): final train loss 3.43, 3.38, 3.47, 3.54 and 3.41 for Transformer, RMT, Hierarchical Aggregation, Depthwise LSTM and Highway Transformer, at 134M–233M parameters.

record.verdict_notes: Fig. 2 uses train loss and spans only about one order of magnitude, so it cannot bear on V1 or V2 as worded. The RMT Dk sweep changes an architecture detail at fixed parameters. Loss moves by about 5% across that sweep, but this is a novel memory-matrix dimension rather than depth or width, so it is not linked to V4.

versions.untested_parts: No test of held-out pretraining loss as a power law in parameters, tokens, or compute over several orders of magnitude. The reported scaling curves use training loss, and the residual-stream sweep varies a different axis.
No small-run fit or prediction of the loss of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute search for the loss-minimising parameter/token split or fitted growth trends for either quantity.
No controlled sweep of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count to test their effect on loss.
No other modality or training regime is tested for the same power-law form.
Downstream evaluations compare RMT and Transformer models, but do not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents, and no test of whether curves bend away from a single power law.
